claim: COVID-19 took away critical training opportunities from those looking to enter the industries.

quotes: I can add to that the education bodies that trained artists and technicians and designers online over COVID. They are coming into our theatre because we are a training ground for those people, and their physical skill knowledge is so below what it would have been had they been able to do practical work. That then leaves them with anxiety because they do not know or, you know, then they are leaving the industry.
Nadja KOSTICH: Just extrapolating on that point, with the loss of our industry people and the coming up of young, emerging artists, those that are remaining are really stretched.
detail.critic_finding: The source says COVID shifted training online and degraded practical skills, not that it took away training opportunities altogether. The claim overstates by implying access was removed rather than diminished in quality.
detail.source_says: COVID forced training online, resulting in graduates with significantly below-standard practical/physical skills, causing anxiety and some to leave the industry — but training itself continued, just in degraded form.
detail.so_what: Reader would think COVID blocked entry to training entirely; source says it degraded quality of practical training for those who did train.

claim: COVID-19 led to worsening mental health in the industries, particularly among children and young people.

quotes: We are also finding that families have slowly returned. It was a strange thing to run workshops on performing arts via Zoom, but we did it to keep our community going and to keep our artists employed. Upon return it has slowly trickled up in terms of attendance, but the edge has been taken off. We have had families that are not able to afford the enrolment fees. Some of our young people come in by enrolment. We then have a series of scholarships and we need to provide more scholarships than we ever have.
I think we have all experienced that in our own families.

There is that ongoing effect of people being nervous about staying in an industry that is so volatile, and parts of the arts sector were not supported through COVID, so they have disappeared. The lack of technical people that can do technical work – they have left the industry because they were not supported.

a pattern of financial precarity and its relationship to poor mental health among culturally and linguistically diverse Victorians. Financial precarity was already an issue for artists generally before the COVID lockdowns, but the intensity and duration of lockdowns in Melbourne significantly depressed the creative economy, and the ensuing cost of living as well as housing affordability has resulted in high rates of depression and mental health and wellbeing issues among these groups.
detail.critic_finding: Multiple witnesses explicitly testified that COVID-19 worsened mental health across the creative industries, with particular emphasis on children and young people experiencing increased anxiety, depression and social disconnection.

claim: Victoria receives its fair share of funding from Creative Australia.

quotes: From our analysis of that – and this is just Creative Australia – Victoria is the only state or territory that is getting exactly its fair share on a per capita basis. You have 26 per cent of the population, and our analysis shows that you are getting 26 per cent of Creative Australia money.
I would say that one of the real barriers in this space is a lack of understanding of what levels of government can do what and where different types of investment are focused and why.
The short answer is yes, and the longer answer is there is interest in this.

David DAVIS: But when you take into account the other arts organisations – we had SBS here yesterday, and we have got a very small percentage of their funding in Victoria, and the ABC, and then you can move to others – it becomes a different situation. Kate FIELDING: Absolutely, and that takes us back to the bigger point, which is that we do not have visibility on cultural funding by government.
detail.critic_finding: Kate Fielding (ANA) confirmed Victoria gets exactly its per-capita share from Creative Australia specifically, but explicitly noted this covers only ~3% of total cultural spend and does not account for ABC, SBS, or other federal streams where Victoria appears under-represented.
detail.source_says: Victoria receives its per-capita share of Creative Australia funding specifically (26% of population, 26% of Creative Australia money), but this is only one small part of total federal cultural spending, and Victoria's share of broader federal cultural expenditure is unknown due to data not being released by jurisdiction.
detail.so_what: Reader would miss that "fair share" applies only to Creative Australia grants, not total federal cultural spending, where Victoria's share is unknown and likely lower.

claim: Regional Victoria does not receive its fair share of funding from Creative Australia.

quotes: From our analysis of that – and this is just Creative Australia – Victoria is the only state or territory that is getting exactly its fair share on a per capita basis. You have 26 per cent of the population, and our analysis shows that you are getting 26 per cent of Creative Australia money.

regional Victoria continues to demonstrate significant unrealised potential across all art forms and that there is an enormous opportunity to translate further investment into impact across the Victorian economy

when we cut the data from Creative Australia by region using the accessibility/remoteness index of Australia – ARIA – definition, which has 40 per cent of Australians living in regional Australia, the total of Creative Australia's investment that goes to regional is 17 per cent, so 23 per cent less than what they should be getting.
regional Victorians receive $1.06 per capita compared to $3.79 per capita in other states
detail.critic_finding: Victoria overall gets its per-capita share from Creative Australia per ANA and Creative Victoria. The underfunding claim is true only for regional areas specifically, and the regional shortfall is a nationwide phenomenon, not unique to Victoria.
detail.source_says: Regional Victoria (and regional Australia generally) receives far less than its population share from Creative Australia (17% vs 40% of population regionally nationwide), but Victoria as a whole receives approximately its per-capita share.
detail.so_what: Reader would think Victoria overall is underfunded by Creative Australia; actually only regional Victoria (not Victoria as a whole) is shortchanged, and the regional shortfall is a national pattern, not Victoria-specific.

claim: Regional Victoria receives its fair share of funding from Creative Australia.

quotes: From our analysis of that – and this is just Creative Australia – Victoria is the only state or territory that is getting exactly its fair share on a per capita basis. You have 26 per cent of the population, and our analysis shows that you are getting 26 per cent of Creative Australia money.

The only other point I would make, and again it is with my regional hat on, is that when we cut the data from Creative Australia by region using the accessibility/remoteness index of Australia – ARIA – definition, which has 40 per cent of Australians living in regional Australia, the total of Creative Australia's investment that goes to regional is 17 per cent, so 23 per cent less than what they should be getting.
In the most recent round Victoria's public galleries shared in 3 per cent of the funding on offer.
Absolutely inadequate.
detail.critic_finding: Kate Fielding (ANA) explicitly stated that while Victoria as a whole gets its per-capita share from Creative Australia, regional Victoria receives only 17% of Creative Australia investment versus 40% population share — a 23% shortfall. Other witnesses (Regional Arts Victoria, PGAV, Jo Porter) also called regional funding "absolutely inadequate."
detail.so_what: A reader would think regional Victoria is equitably funded by Creative Australia, when witnesses consistently said it receives far less than its population share.

claim: Witnesses said ticket prices have fallen since 2019.

quotes: 2.1 million fewer people have attended fewer events in the last five years, with 47 per cent citing the ticket prices and 38 per cent citing the cost of living as a cause.
A cost-of-living crisis means that while audiences are returning, ticket prices remain stagnant, limiting income.
the barrier I think is money. It is ticket prices. I am sorry to be so simple about it, but I think if there were cheaper tickets or low-cost tickets, people would go to more shows.
detail.critic_finding: No witness said ticket prices fell. Witnesses consistently described prices as stagnant, too high, or a barrier to attendance — the opposite of a fall.
detail.so_what: Readers would think ticket prices dropped, when witnesses said they are stagnant or unaffordably high, driving people away.

claim: According to Claire Febey of Creative Victoria, COVID-19 led to worsening mental health in the industries, particularly among children and young people.

detail.critic_finding: Claire Febey's testimony does not include statements about COVID-19 worsening mental health among children and young people. That evidence came from other witnesses (e.g., Nadja Kostich, Katrina Cornwell, Debra Allanson).
detail.so_what: Reader would think Creative Victoria's CEO made this claim; she did not — other witnesses did.
